title: 3-Read Friday #27: Calling Out, Do Now Activities, and Multitasking
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 27 is anchored in real-time classroom observation: Barton introduces Adam Boxer's "Calling out calling out" by describing a Year 11 lesson he watched that same morning, where a student called out six consecutive answers with no ill intent but visibly frustrated and then deadened the rest of the class, and credits Boxer's concrete strategies with directly shaping the coaching conversation that followed. His second pick, Tom Sherrington's ten problems with Do Now activities, is framed as validation and extension of Barton's own prior work helping a department build a common approach to lesson starters, praised for identifying why Do Nows often fail to deliver the learning impact teachers expect despite achieving a calm start. His third selection, Thahmina Begum's piece on the redundancy effect, prompts an unusually self-critical aside from Barton, who admits he required students to copy worked examples while he talked routinely for roughly twelve years of his own teaching, before crediting Begum's post with clearly explaining why that habit undermines learning. All three picks orbit specific, moment-to-moment classroom interaction patterns rather than broader policy or curriculum questions, giving the issue a tight, classroom-craft focus.
points: Barton's commentary on Adam Boxer's calling-out piece is grounded in a same-day classroom observation - a Year 11 student calling out six consecutive answers - that he explicitly used to shape a coaching conversation immediately afterward.

He frames Tom Sherrington's Do Now critique through his own prior writing on building a departmental approach to lesson starters, positioning Sherrington's piece as validating and extending work he'd already done.

Barton's response to Thahmina Begum's multitasking piece includes a rare self-critical admission - that he personally had students copy worked examples while he talked routinely for about twelve years of his own teaching career.
All three picks this issue concern moment-to-moment classroom interaction patterns rather than assessment, leadership, or curriculum design.
quotes: I love this series of posts by Adam, and this one has come at just the right time. This morning, I watched a Year 11 lesson where a girl called out the answer to 6 questions in a row.

The girl didn’t think she was doing anything wrong; indeed, she was just being keen and enthusiastic. But the effect it had on the rest of the class was palpable. Some were frustrated, most descended into apathy.
I am obsessed with the start of lessons. I recently wrote a post on the work I did with a department to develop a common approach to the Do Now.
This from Tom is excellent in how it gets right at the heart of why some Do Nows take so long and don’t have the impact on learning that teachers hope.

One of my pet hates is when I watch a lesson and the students are asked to copy down a worked example while the teacher is talking and modelling themselves. It annoys me so much because I did this routinely in my classroom for about 12 years.
In this post, Thahmina reinforces exactly why asking students to write and listen simultaneously is problematic, and suggests some concrete actions we can take to avoid it happening.
